intro: Seven drawings, one belt. Scroll and it runs.

chapters.title: Robots that handle DNA
chapters.text: I studied bioengineering at UC Santa Cruz, then built and programmed liquid-handling robots for synthetic DNA manufacturing. I also invented the first process for recovering monoclonal DNA clusters from Illumina flow cells.

chapters.title: A belt that opens and closes
chapters.text: I founded Veer to make belt drivetrains for bikes. I invented Split Belt Pro and the V-Link detachable belt splice, which created the first belt-drive conversion category for cycling and won the Eurobike Startup Award, competing against Gates.

chapters.title: The rig that found the failure
chapters.text: Our early belts failed. In one week I built a drivetrain test suite that goes beyond ISO standards, including a universal testing machine made from a log splitter and a load cell. It found the root cause, and the redesigned belt lasts 20,000 miles.

chapters.title: Shifting under load
chapters.text: SHIFT is a seamless belt transmission that shifts under load, without a clutch. I invented it, wrote and prosecuted the patent myself to grant in the US and internationally with no rejections, and designed it for manufacture.

chapters.title: Ten minutes down to thirty seconds
chapters.text: Putting a belt together took about 10 minutes. I designed and programmed LinkBot, an automated belt-assembly tool that does it in under 30 seconds, with fewer than 1 fault per 4,000 rivets.

chapters.title: A shop for same-day parts
chapters.text: I built a prototyping shop around five CNC machines, set up for same-day design-to-testable-part, and invented the LavaLock universal workholding system: 91% less setup time and 50% lower prototype cost. We machined next-day prototypes for aerospace and robotics customers, including Zipline.

chapters.title: Nine prototypes, all flown
chapters.text: On Zipline's New Products team I took the second-generation Dropbox, a robotic drone-loading and package-pickup kiosk, from rough sketches through 9 flight-tested prototypes across 3 generations. The results: more than 10x improvement in key package-pickup reliability metrics, and about 3x lower cost than the current production generation.
